title: Electoral vs Liberal Democracy
hook: Holding elections isn't the whole of democracy. Without rights, courts, and limits on the winner, voting alone can deliver an elected strongman.
key_points: Electoral democracy means leaders are chosen through regular, competitive elections.
Liberal democracy adds constitutional limits: rights, rule of law, and independent courts.
Elections decide who governs; liberal constraints decide what they may not do.
An 'illiberal democracy' holds elections but erodes rights and checks on the winners.
content_html: It is tempting to equate democracy with elections, but the two are not the same, and the gap between them explains a great deal of modern politics. Electoral democracy refers to the procedure for choosing rulers: regular, competitive elections in which voters can replace those in power. Liberal democracy is electoral democracy plus a set of constraints on what any winner may do — protected individual rights, the rule of law, and independent institutions such as courts and a free press that hold power in check between elections.
extra_html: The cleanest way to hold the distinction is this: elections decide who governs, while liberal-constitutional limits decide what they may not do regardless of how big their majority. Encyclopaedia Britannica discusses this under constitutionalism — the principle that government power is defined and bounded by a higher law. The distinction matters because the two components can come apart. A country can hold genuine elections yet steadily strip away rights, neuter the courts, and silence critics — a combination often labeled "illiberal democracy." Such a system retains the legitimacy of the ballot box while removing the protections that stop a majority, or a popular leader, from oppressing minorities and entrenching themselves. Recognizing that elections are necessary but not sufficient is the key insight: durable democracy requires not just the right to vote, but the rights and limits that make sure today's winners cannot make themselves impossible to vote out tomorrow.

related.title: What Democracy Means
related.hook: Rule by the people: a system where political power ultimately traces back to citizens, usually through regular, free elections.

related.title: Democracy vs Authoritarianism
related.hook: The deepest dividing line between regimes isn't left versus right — it's whether power can be lost. Can the people remove their rulers, or not?

related.title: Equality & Minority Rights
related.hook: Majority rule can become majority tyranny. Equality before the law and minority rights are how democracies stop the many from trampling the few.

related.title: Democratic Backsliding
related.hook: Democracies rarely die in a single coup anymore. More often they erode — legally, gradually, step by step — until little is left but the shell of elections.

flashcards.prompt: What does liberal democracy add to electoral democracy?
flashcards.back_html: Constitutional limits — protected rights, the rule of law, and independent courts — that constrain what election winners may do.

flashcards.prompt: What is the core difference between electoral and liberal democracy?

choices.text: Elections decide who governs; liberal constraints decide what they may not do

flashcards.explanation_html: Electoral democracy is about choosing rulers; liberal democracy adds enforceable limits on those rulers' power.

choices.text: A system that holds elections but erodes rights and checks on the winners
A democracy with unusually strong courts
A country with no elections at all

flashcards.explanation_html: Illiberal democracies keep the form of elections while weakening the rights and institutions that limit those in power.
